flashcards.q: What are the three Core Web Vitals and their "good" thresholds at p75?
flashcards.a: LCP < 2.5s (loading), INP < 200ms (responsiveness, replaced FID in March 2024), CLS < 0.1 (visual stability) -- graded at the 75th percentile of real users over CrUX's rolling 28-day window.

flashcards.q: What are the four phases LCP decomposes into for diagnosis?
flashcards.a: TTFB, resource load delay (TTFB to fetch start), resource load time (the fetch itself), and element render delay (load to actual paint) -- each separately measurable via the web-vitals library's attribution data.

flashcards.q: Why does client-side-rendered LCP image discovery hurt LCP even if the image is small and fast?
flashcards.a: The browser's preload scanner parses raw HTML for resource hints before JS executes; an image only added to the DOM after a JS data fetch is invisible to that early scanner, so its download starts far later than a server-rendered tag would allow.

flashcards.q: What happens when loading="lazy" is applied to the actual LCP image, with real numbers?
flashcards.a: Measured field data: p75 LCP moves from 364ms to 720ms and the share of "good" pages drops from 79% to 52%. Never lazy-load the LCP candidate; do lazy-load everything below the fold.

flashcards.q: What is a "long task" and why does it hurt INP?
flashcards.a: Any main-thread JS execution exceeding 50ms without yielding. During it, the browser can't process input or paint, so an interaction landing mid-task waits for the whole task to finish before input delay even ends.

flashcards.q: What is the prioritized fix order for a slow, INP-hurting click handler?
flashcards.a: 1) Chunk the work and yield back to the browser between chunks (scheduler.yield / setTimeout fallback). 2) Move heavy CPU-bound computation to a Web Worker. 3) Defer non-critical work via requestIdleCallback. 4) Reduce DOM work (virtualize long lists) rather than optimizing per-item render cost.

flashcards.q: Name the three most common real causes of CLS and their fixes.
flashcards.a: 1) Images/embeds without reserved width/height/aspect-ratio -> set them explicitly. 2) Web font swap metric mismatch -> font-display:optional (zero CLS) or size-adjust metric matching. 3) Content injected above existing content post-render -> reserve space or use an overlay.

flashcards.q: Difference between font-display: swap and font-display: optional?
flashcards.a: swap shows fallback text immediately and swaps in the custom font whenever it arrives (good for LCP, risks CLS on swap). optional gives the browser ~100ms to load the font; if it misses, the fallback is used for the entire page view with no later swap -- zero CLS, sometimes no custom font.

flashcards.q: What realistic bundle-size reduction is achievable from route-based code splitting plus tree shaking/dependency swaps?
flashcards.a: An unoptimized SPA bundle around 2-2.5MB can realistically drop 60-80% in total size -- route splitting alone often gets the initial critical-path bundle to roughly 100-150KB, with heavier dependency swaps (e.g. moment.js -> date-fns) compounding the reduction.

flashcards.q: What image format/support numbers matter for LCP strategy as of 2026?
flashcards.a: AVIF is ~50% smaller than JPEG at comparable quality (~95% browser support); WebP is 25-35% smaller (~96% support). Images are ~45-55% of page weight and the LCP element on ~85% of desktop pages -- serve via <picture> with format fallbacks, not a single format.

flashcards.q: What measured impact does fetchpriority="high" have on LCP, per Google's own tests?
flashcards.a: Cut LCP from 2.6s to 1.9s on a representative page when applied to the LCP image alone.

flashcards.q: Why can two pages have identical Lighthouse scores but very different real-world INP?
flashcards.a: Lighthouse runs a fixed, short interaction script on a simulated device profile and doesn't capture real session length or accumulated page state (memory growth, a list grown large through use) that field INP reflects; the difference only surfaces in RUM attribution data, not a cold lab run.

flashcards.q: Why is a CI Lighthouse win with no corresponding CrUX field-data change three weeks later not necessarily a failed fix?
flashcards.a: CrUX uses a rolling 28-day window, so a fix needs real user traffic to accumulate before the reported number moves -- three weeks may not be enough data yet depending on traffic volume, separate from any lab-vs-field profile mismatch.
